newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Author O'Rourke sees media madness in HK handover.
newsitem.headline: Author O'Rourke sees media madness in HK handover.

text.p: Hong Kong's handover is a huge growth industry for the world's media, American humourist P.J. O'Rourke says, but is otherwise a "non-event".

"The handover is a great thing -- for journalists. And a great thing for journalists should make other people nervous," he said to laughs from a luncheon crowd at the Foreign Correspondents' Club on Friday.

With more than 8,000 journalists descending on Hong Kong to report on the British territory's return to Chinese rule on July 1, O'Rourke said handovers should be held regularly all over the world as a "full-employment programme" for the media.
But he took his "fellow hacks" to task for not being critical enough of China, which he described as "not exactly a living festival of the Bill of Rights".
"Are we being tough enough on this story? Is there just a little bit of Beijing cuddle-bunny going on here?" said O'Rourke, who is on his second visit to Hong Kong.

But O'Rourke -- renowned for his caustic wit and perverse take on world events as the roving foreign affairs chief for "Rolling Stone" magazine and the author of "Holidays in Hell", "Republican Party Reptiles" and six other books -- said he would be giving the handover a miss.
"Rolling Stone" forgot to apply for his media accreditation and, besides, he was planning to take it easy when the Union Jack is lowered for the last time at midnight on June 30.
"I'll be asleep," he said. "I'm 50 and this is a non-event."
O'Rourke, whose next stop is Albania, said there were alternatives to Britain handing back the free-wheeling, capitalist territory to communist China -- including a takeover bid by Hong Kong.
"Why didn't they just buy England? They can afford it," he said.

Or Britain could have handed over England to the Chinese leaders, who are "far more market-oriented" than new Labour Prime Minister Tony Blair and "have experience dealing with royal family problems", he said.
And his advice to post-handover leader Tung Chee-hwa?
"Keep mahjong legal if you want things peaceful."
